cheatsheet.title: Hash map lookups
points: Trade O(n) extra space for O(n) time
Store what you have seen; ask for what you need

patterns.name: Complement lookup
patterns.whenToUse: Pairs that must combine to a target (sum, difference, XOR).

questions.title: Two Sum
questions.prompt:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the **indices** of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

Exactly one valid answer exists and you may not use the same element twice.
hints: The brute force checks every pair. Which work is repeated?
For each number x you need exactly target − x. How can you check if you've already seen it in O(1)?
Store each value → index in a hash map as you scan; look up the complement before inserting.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every pair (i, j) with i < j and return the first that sums to target.

approaches.name: Sort + two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort (value, index) pairs and move two pointers inward. Works, but sorting costs O(n log n) and you must keep original indices.

approaches.name: One-pass hash map
approaches.idea: Scan once; for each x, check whether target − x is already in the map, otherwise record x → index.

solution.summary: Scan once with a hash map from value to index; for each number check if its complement (target − x) was already seen.
solution.explanation:
Every pair that sums to `target` has a **complement** relationship: if we are at `x`, the partner must be `target − x`.

1. Keep a map `seen` from value → index of everything to the **left** of the current position.
2. At index `i`, compute `need = target − nums[i]`.
3. If `need` is in `seen`, the answer is `[seen[need], i]`.
4. Otherwise store `nums[i] → i` and continue.

Checking *before* inserting guarantees we never pair an element with itself, and duplicates like `[3, 3]` still work because the first 3 is already stored when we reach the second.

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass, O(1) average per map operation
complexity.space: O(n) — the map can hold every element

keyPoints: State the brute force O(n²) first, then optimise
Hash map trades O(n) space for O(n) time
Check for the complement before inserting the current value
Mention the sort + two-pointer alternative and why it is worse here (loses indices, O(n log n))

visuals.title: One-pass hash map on nums = [3, 8, 4, 1, 6], target = 10
visuals.caption: Blue = current index, green = the answer pair. The map on the right holds every value seen so far.

steps.note: Start with an empty map `seen` (value → index).
i = 0: need = 10 − 3 = 7. 7 is not in `seen`, so store 3 → 0.
i = 4: need = 10 − 6 = 4, and **4 is in `seen` at index 2**. Return [2, 4].

pitfalls: Inserting before checking can pair an element with itself (e.g. target 6, nums[i] = 3)
Sorting the array destroys the original indices

followUps.question: What if the array is already sorted?
followUps.answer: Use two pointers from both ends: O(n) time, O(1) space.

followUps.question: What if you must return all unique pairs?
followUps.answer: Sort, then two pointers while skipping duplicates, or use a set of seen values and a set of emitted pairs.

questions.title: TCP vs UDP — what is the difference?
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between **TCP** and **UDP**. When would you choose each?
hints: Think about guarantees: ordering, delivery, connection setup.
What does each guarantee cost in latency and overhead?

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "TCP is reliable, UDP is fast." True but shallow — no mechanisms, no examples.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Compare connection setup, reliability mechanisms (ACKs, retransmission, sequence numbers), flow/congestion control, header size, and give real use cases.

solution.summary: TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery using a handshake, sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission; UDP is connectionless, sends independent datagrams with no guarantees, and is used when low latency matters more than reliability.
solution.explanation:
**TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)**
- Opens a connection with a **3-way handshake** (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK).
- Numbers every byte, acknowledges received data and **retransmits** lost segments, so data arrives complete and in order.
- Has **flow control** (receiver window) and **congestion control** (slow start, AIMD).
- Byte-stream; 20–60 byte header.
- Used by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, SSH, SMTP, database connections.

**UDP (User Datagram Protocol)**
- No handshake, no connection state — just send datagrams.
- No ordering, no retransmission; a lost packet is simply gone.
- 8 byte header, very low overhead and latency.
- Used by DNS lookups, video calls, online games, live streaming, and QUIC (HTTP/3 builds reliability on top of UDP).
keyPoints: TCP = connection + reliability + ordering + flow/congestion control
Choose UDP when stale data is useless (voice, games) or for tiny request/response (DNS)

visuals.title: TCP vs UDP at a glance
rows: Datagrams may arrive out of order

frames.note: TCP needs a 3-way handshake before any data flows.
frames.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: SYN (seq = x)
    S->>C: SYN-ACK (seq = y, ack = x + 1)
    C->>S: ACK (ack = y + 1)
    Note over C,S: Connection established
    C->>S: Data

frames.note: UDP sends immediately — no setup, no acknowledgements.
frames.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: Datagram 1
    C->>S: Datagram 2
    Note over C,S: No ACKs, lost datagrams are not resent

pitfalls: Saying UDP is "unreliable so never used" — DNS, video and HTTP/3 depend on it

followUps.question: How does HTTP/3 get reliability over UDP?
followUps.answer: QUIC implements its own streams, ACKs, retransmission and TLS 1.3 handshake in user space on top of UDP, avoiding TCP head-of-line blocking.

quiz.question: What is the average time complexity of a hash map lookup?
quiz.explanation: Hashing jumps directly to a bucket; collisions are rare on average, so lookups are O(1) average (O(n) worst case).

quiz.question: Which protocol does DNS primarily use for normal queries?
quiz.explanation: DNS queries are small request/response pairs, so UDP on port 53 is used; TCP is used for large responses and zone transfers.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: Map keys use SameValueZero equality, so the number 1 and the string '1' are different keys.
